newsitem.title: USA: Consumer groups want tougher U.S. bank regulations.
newsitem.headline: Consumer groups want tougher U.S. bank regulations.

text.p: With Congress working to overhaul U.S. banking laws, consumer advocacy groups reminded legislators on Tuesday not to leave out strong consumer protection.

"While we understand the desire of various industries to expand their financial services activities and the need to modernize banking laws, such expansion will not benefit consumers unless protections are in place to address the current and likely abuses in the market," Mary Griffin, counsel for Consumers Union, told a Congressional subcommittee hearing.

The hearing of the House Banking Committee's financial institutions subcommittee was considering the merits of allowing banks to offer insurance and securities products, while allowing firms from those two industries into banking.

Consumers Union, publisher of Consumer Reports magazine, and other groups said numerous safeguards were needed to prevent banks and other institutions from misleading consumers about the applicability of federal deposit insurance. Consumers seeking loans were also in danger of being coerced into buying other services, the groups said.
Existing consumer protections, and those included in the new bill, are inadequate, the groups warned.
For example, consumers overpaid at least $400 million a year for credit life insurance, according to the U.S. Public Interest Research Group.
The product, which covers consumer debt in case of death, is often sold in conjuction with credit card offers.
"Some banks in some states have sold savings bank life insurance for years, generally at competitive rates," Edmund Mierzwinski, consumer program director for the group, told the subcommittee.
But, Mierzwinski added, "Banks are also among the firms, along with car dealers and small loan companies, which profit from an egregious and over-priced product -- credit life insurance."
Consumers Union said the Securities and Exchange Commission should be given more authority over banks' securities activities.
Banks should also be required to separate sales of non-banking products from areas where insured deposits are handled, Consumers Union said.
Some of the groups, along with former Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker, also urged Congress to reject proposals that would allow non-financial companies into banking, insurance and securities.

One bill under consideration would allow financial companies to conduct 25 percent of their business in non-financial, commercial activities. Another bill would impose no limits, allowing banks to own or be owned by commercial companies.

"Failure by the Congress to seize this opportunity to modernize the legislative framework for banking and finance would be sad indeed," Volcker said. "But I also have to say none of that would be worth the risks and costs of embarking on a new experiment -- an experiment foreign to our traditions and experience -- of relaxing prohibition on combinations of banking and commerce."
